Without any corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal content involving war, military, or ethnic/geographic conflict, this item appears clinically incoherent for this patient.

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Strictly restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other selected items coherently describe PTSD related to partner physical abuse (criticism, violence, offender cues; fragmented/alien memory; rage; dehumanization, self-blame, emotional numbing; distraction and cue avoidance). In contrast, restrictive eating introduces a distinct control-focused coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in triggers, memory, threat, or appraisals, making it clinically hard to explain as part of the same formulation rather than a separate problem.

vignette:
Tane

Tane had been editing manuscripts for forty-three years when everything fractured. At seventy-four, he had built a reputation in academic publishing for precision and grace—the kind of editor authors requested by name, who could reshape a paragraph without diminishing its author's voice. His apartment in Portland overlooked the Columbia River, lined with first editions and the accumulated trust of two decades of professional relationships. He had learned early that control over language meant control over meaning, and control over meaning meant safety. This belief had sustained him through a marriage that ended quietly, through the ordinary solitudes of aging, through the careful architecture of a life lived mostly alone.

Then Marcus had arrived. Marcus was fifteen years younger, charming in a way that made Tane's caution seem like unnecessary armor. They met at a book launch in the spring of 2019. For eight months, Tane allowed himself to believe that the distance he had maintained for so long might finally ease. He was wrong about what that would cost.

The violence came without warning on a February evening. They had been discussing an article Marcus had written—something about labor practices in the film industry. Tane had suggested a structural revision, nothing harsh, the kind of feedback he gave to strangers every day. Marcus had stood abruptly, his face darkening, and said Tane was always correcting him, always implying he wasn't good enough. When Tane tried to clarify, Marcus moved toward him with a speed that erased the distance between them. The first blow came to Tane's ribs. He remembered it not as a continuous assault but as a series of isolated moments: Marcus's fist, the wall behind him, his own hands raised in a useless gesture of protection, Marcus's face contorted with something Tane had never seen before. Then Marcus was gone, and Tane was alone on the floor, breathing in shallow gasps, his mind fragmenting the experience into discrete, unconnected images.

He did not report it. He told himself it was an aberration, that Marcus had been under stress, that Tane's suggestion had been poorly timed. This reasoning—the belief that the violence had happened because of something in Tane himself, some failure of judgment or sensitivity—took root and hardened. When Marcus called the next day with apologies and flowers, Tane accepted both. When it happened again three weeks later, triggered again by what Tane perceived as a minor criticism, Tane had already begun to reconstruct the narrative: he was the sort of person this happened to. He was the sort of person who provoked it.

The relationship lasted another six months before collapsing entirely. But the damage had already metastasized. Tane found that criticism of any kind—a colleague's gentle suggestion about a manuscript, an author's polite pushback on his edits—sent him into a state of hypervigilance. His chest would tighten. He would see Marcus's face. He began to distract himself obsessively: checking email, reorganizing files, anything to interrupt the moment when someone might correct him. He stopped attending editorial meetings. He began declining projects that required collaboration.

At home, he had removed everything that reminded him of Marcus: the photographs, the books Marcus had given him, even the wine glasses they had used together. But the avoidance extended further. He stopped listening to music—certain songs had played during their time together. He stopped allowing himself to feel anything intensely. When his sister called with news of a family death, he felt nothing, and this numbness terrified him more than the rage did. The rage came when he remembered those fragmented moments: his body on the floor, Marcus's voice, the specific angle of light through the window. The fury that arose was so consuming that he had learned to suppress any thought that might trigger it.

By 2024, Tane's professional life had contracted significantly. He was taking fewer projects, working almost entirely remotely, communicating primarily through email to minimize direct interaction. His editor colleagues had stopped asking him to collaborate. His income had declined. More painfully, he had begun to experience himself as something other than a person—a mechanism for processing text, a thing that occupied space. When he looked in the mirror, he did not recognize the man looking back.

It was his sister who finally insisted he seek help. She had noticed him flinching when she corrected his grammar during a phone call. She had seen him change the channel when a scene of conflict appeared on television. She recognized in her brother's careful, diminished existence the architecture of someone who had learned to take up as little space as possible. Tane had come to believe that he would never feel like himself again, that whatever had been broken in February 2019 could not be repaired. But he had also begun to wonder, in the quietest part of himself, whether it was possible to be human again—to feel something other than rage or numbness, to accept a correction without believing it was a prelude to violence, to exist as something more than an object moving through the world.
